words.definition: To keep a person or thing apart from others in isolation.
words.example: The jury was sequestered in a hotel so no news could reach them.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'seek + rest' — you seek rest by tucking yourself away where no one can find you.

words.definition: Existing or done alone, without any others present.
words.example: A solitary lighthouse keeper spent months without ever seeing another human being.
words.mnemonic: Starts with 'sol' (sun) — picture a single sun hanging in an empty sky, all by itself.

words.definition: The state of being by oneself, away from other people.
words.example: After the noisy party, she craved the solitude of a long, quiet walk.
words.mnemonic: 'Sol' (sun) + 'attitude' — a sunny attitude you enjoy entirely on your own.

words.definition: To split something into separate pieces or break it apart forcefully.
words.example: The earthquake sundered the highway, leaving a gaping crack between the two halves.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'thunder' — imagine a thunderbolt ripping the sky violently in two.

words.definition: A small piece broken off or detached from a larger whole.
words.example: Archaeologists pieced together a shattered vase from dozens of tiny fragments.
words.mnemonic: Shares 'frag' with 'fracture' — a fracture always leaves little broken bits behind.

words.definition: A barrier or division that separates one area into smaller sections.
words.example: A thin partition split the open office into two cramped little rooms.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'part' — a partition literally carves one space into separate parts.

words.definition: To spread out or drive apart across a wide area.
words.example: Police used loudspeakers to disperse the crowd before it grew unruly.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-' (apart) + 'perse' like a 'purse' tipping over so coins fly apart everywhere.

words.definition: To throw or spread things loosely in many directions.
words.example: The autumn wind scattered the leaves across the entire lawn.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'shatter' — when glass shatters, the pieces fly off every which way.

words.definition: To formally break up a group so it no longer exists.
words.example: After the war ended, the militia was ordered to disband and return home.
words.mnemonic: 'Dis-' (undo) + 'band' — undo the band, and the whole group falls apart.

words.definition: To pull back, remove, or retreat from a place or commitment.
words.example: Feeling overwhelmed, he chose to withdraw from the competition at the last minute.
words.mnemonic: 'With-' + 'draw' — you draw yourself back, pulling away from the action.

words.definition: Unfriendly and distant in manner, reluctant to be warm or sociable.
words.example: New colleagues found her standoffish until they realized she was simply shy.
words.mnemonic: Picture someone who 'stands off' at a distance instead of stepping in close.

words.definition: So distant or intimidating that others feel unable to come near or speak.
words.example: The stern professor seemed so unapproachable that students rarely asked him questions.
words.mnemonic: Break it up: 'un-' + 'approach' + '-able' — you are NOT able to walk up to this person.

words.definition: To hold or stick together as a consistent, unified whole.
words.example: The team's scattered ideas finally began to cohere into a single workable plan.
words.mnemonic: 'Co-' (together) + 'here' — everyone stays right here together, clinging as one.

words.definition: To bring separate things together into a single whole.
words.example: A common enemy can unify bitter rivals into one determined alliance.
words.mnemonic: 'Uni' means one — to unify is to fold the many down into one.

words.definition: A deep sharing of thoughts, feelings, or fellowship among people.
words.example: Sitting quietly beneath the trees, she felt a peaceful communion with nature.
words.mnemonic: Hides 'common' + 'union' — a common union of spirits sharing one another deeply.

words.definition: To create or shape something strong and lasting through effort or heat.
words.example: The soldiers forged a lifelong friendship during their years of service.
words.mnemonic: A blacksmith's FORGE: metal heated in fire and hammered into a solid new shape.

words.definition: To combine different elements so they cross and blend together.
words.example: The author interweaves real history and invented characters throughout her novel.
words.mnemonic: inter- (between) + weave: threads passing between one another on a loom.

words.definition: To twist or wrap two or more things around each other.
words.example: The ivy slowly entwined itself around the old stone pillar.
words.mnemonic: en- + twine (string): picture string twisting tightly around something.

words.definition: To link two or more things by twisting them closely together.
words.example: Their fingers intertwined as they walked along the moonlit beach.
words.mnemonic: inter- (between) + twine: two hands' fingers looping between each other.

words.definition: To join people or things closely together into a unified whole.
words.example: Years of shared hardship knit the small village into one family.
words.mnemonic: Picture knitting needles looping loose yarn into a single connected fabric.

words.definition: To include or absorb something as part of a larger whole.
words.example: The chef incorporated fresh basil into the simmering sauce.
words.mnemonic: in- + corpor- (Latin corpus, 'body'): taking something into the body.

words.definition: To combine elements so completely they seem like one thing.
words.example: The band melds jazz and hip-hop into a genuinely fresh sound.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'melt' + 'weld': things melting and welding into one.

words.definition: To join or blend things together, often by heat, into one unit.
words.example: Intense heat fused the two metal plates into a single sheet.
words.mnemonic: Think of metals melting under a lit fuse and running together into one.

words.definition: To come together into a group or crowd in one place.
words.example: Fans congregated outside the stadium hours before kickoff.
words.mnemonic: con- (together) + greg- (Latin flock): a flock gathering, like a congregation.

words.definition: To gather closely together in a small, tight group.
words.example: The children clustered around the storyteller to hear every word.
words.mnemonic: Picture a cluster of grapes: many small things bunched tightly on one stem.

words.definition: To crowd together in large numbers, filling a space.
words.example: Shoppers thronged the market on the final day of the sale.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'strong': a strong, dense mass of people pressing together.

words.definition: To share thoughts or feelings in a close, intimate way.
words.example: She hiked alone into the hills to commune quietly with nature.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'communicate': deep sharing of what you hold in common.

words.definition: To mix together or socialize with many different people.
words.example: Guests mingled freely, drifting from one conversation to another.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'mix' + 'jingle': people mixing and jingling around a party.

words.definition: To regularly keep company or associate with certain people.
words.example: The senator was criticized for consorting with known criminals.
words.mnemonic: con- (with) + sort: spending your time with your own 'sort' of people.

words.definition: To form a close connection or relationship with someone.
words.example: The new puppy quickly bonded with the youngest child in the house.
words.mnemonic: Think of glue or a tie of trust: a bond holds two things firmly together.

words.definition: Impossible to stop, slow down, or persuade away from its course.
words.example: The glacier's inexorable advance crushed everything in its path, indifferent to our pleas.
words.mnemonic: In-EX-orable — 'in' (not) + 'exorable' (able to be begged); you cannot beg it to change.

words.definition: To voluntarily let go of something you hold, own, or control.
words.example: After forty years at the helm, the founder finally relinquished the company to his daughter.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'reling-quish' — picture your hand un-clenching and letting the reins slip away.

words.definition: To deliberately stay away from something on principle or by choice.
words.example: A committed minimalist, she eschews clutter and owns barely a dozen possessions.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'es-CHEW' — like sneezing 'achoo' at something you refuse to touch or chew.

words.definition: To catch or involve someone deeply in something difficult to escape.
words.example: One small favor enmeshed him in a web of debts he could never repay.
words.mnemonic: en + MESH — trapped inside a net's mesh, tangled and unable to break free.

words.definition: The practice of giving and receiving benefits equally between two sides.
words.example: Their friendship thrived on reciprocity: every favor was quietly returned in kind.
words.mnemonic: Root 'reciproc-' as in 'recipe' shared back and forth — I cook for you, you cook for me.

words.definition: To separate or disconnect one thing from another in your mind.
words.example: The company scrambled to dissociate its brand from the scandal engulfing its former partner.
words.mnemonic: dis- (apart) + 'associate' — undo the association, pull the two apart.

words.definition: An amount so large it becomes excessive or sickening.
words.example: After the holidays, a surfeit of chocolate left the children queasy and sick of sweets.
words.mnemonic: 'Sir Fit' ate so much at the feast that a SURFEIT made him unfit.

words.definition: Lacking the power to move or the will to act.
words.example: The patient lay inert on the couch, too exhausted to lift even a finger.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-hurt' but really 'in-ert' — an INERT gas won't react; it just sits still.

words.definition: To spread through every part of something, often gradually and completely.
words.example: The smell of fresh bread permeated the whole house within minutes.
words.mnemonic: per- (through) + 'meate' like 'meet' — it goes through to meet every corner.

words.definition: To be present and felt throughout all of a place or thing.
words.example: A quiet sense of dread pervaded the empty station as midnight approached.
words.mnemonic: per- (through) + 'vade' (go, as in 'invade') — it goes through and invades everywhere.

words.definition: To gradually spread color, light, or feeling across a surface or space.
words.example: A warm pink glow suffused the sky as the sun slipped below the hills.
words.mnemonic: suf- (under) + 'fuse' — light gets fused underneath everything, flooding it softly.

words.definition: To fill someone or something deeply with a quality or feeling.
words.example: Her grandmother's stories imbued her with a lifelong love of the sea.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'im-BREW' — steep a teabag until the water is brewed full of flavor.

words.definition: Cold, bare, and offering no warmth, comfort, or hope.
words.example: The job outlook was so bleak that graduates were leaving the town entirely.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'weak' and 'bleach' — a BLEAK moor is bleached grey, weak of life.

words.definition: A person who lives alone and avoids contact with others.
words.example: The famous author became a recluse, refusing all interviews and seeing almost no one.
words.mnemonic: re- (back) + 'cluse' (closed, like 'seclude') — someone closed away from the world.

words.definition: Sealed so completely that no air or outside influence can enter.
words.example: The rare manuscripts are kept in a hermetic vault where humidity never fluctuates.
words.mnemonic: From Hermes Trismegistus, whose 'hermetic seal' locked out all air — airtight and closed off.

words.definition: To stick firmly to a surface, or to follow a rule, plan, or belief closely.
words.example: The nurse pressed the bandage down so it would adhere to his skin despite the sweat.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-HERE' — glue keeps something right HERE, stuck in place.

words.definition: To come together or bring people together for a formal meeting or purpose.
words.example: The committee will convene at nine to vote on the new budget.
words.mnemonic: Break it as 'con-VENE' — think 'come + venue': people arrive at a venue together.
